speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our proposals in this debate are based on accepting the existence of GRCs as reality and how we can make things better within that reality and is not an indication of a change of position on GRCs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On previous occasions, the Prime Minister has only revealed to the public that the EBRC has been formed months after he has convened the EBRC.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the interests of transparency and public accountability, I would first like to start by asking the Prime Minister whether he has formed the EBRC.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP has raised this Motion today because we believe that there are many areas in this process which can be reformed, so that electoral boundaries are reviewed in a manner that incorporates transparency, accountability, independence, fairness and respect for voters.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, justify boundary changes for transparency and accountability.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The EBRC needs to make public the reasons why the boundaries of certain constituencies are changed while others remain untouched.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over the years, the reports of the EBRC have become shorter and shorter, providing less and less explanation of why the boundaries have changed.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reports of the 2011, 2015 and 2020 EBRCs were only four pages long and contained six paragraphs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, in the 2020 report, the EBRC merely stated, "The Committee reviewed the boundaries of the current electoral divisions taking into account the current configurations, changes in the number of electors due to population shifts and housing developments." This is in stark contrast to the early years of Independence.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The report of the 1971 EBRC, for example, was 12 pages long and contained 20 paragraphs, and provided more details for its decisions than present-day EBRCs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, the 1971 EBRC explained clearly the reasons why it did not alter the boundaries of constituencies in the central areas of the city.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It even explained the names for new constituencies.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many constituencies now have strange boundaries that do not follow the boundaries of Housing and Development Board (HDB) towns or Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) planning areas, or any relation to how people on the ground live their lives.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 1971, the EBRC clearly stated that "all changes and adjustments were made in keeping with proximity, identity of interest and similarity of association".

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These do not appear to be considerations for the EBRCs of today.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is common to find residents of the same HDB town belonging to different constituencies.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I still remember when I first entered politics more than a decade ago, a veteran in an opposition party told me how hard he walked the ground in a Single Member Constituency (SMC) for four years, only to have that SMC disappear on him when boundaries were reviewed and the SMC was absorbed into a GRC.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is this an isolated incident or is there a pattern?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We examined the data on SMCs from GE1988 to GE2015, spanning seven GEs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Excluding opposition-held SMCs at the point of boundary review, we find that amongst the SMCs where opposition scored below 40% of the votes, on average, 58% were retained as SMCs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In comparison, where opposition scored between 40% and 50% of the votes, only 33% were retained on average.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: SMCs in GE2020 cannot be included here because the decision on whether they will be retained is yet to be made.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We hope that these statistics will not be maintained or further aggravated by the next boundary review.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Without clear justifications for its decisions, it is difficult to tell whether the EBRC has changed the boundaries simply because of population shifts and housing developments, or for other reasons.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Suspicions of gerrymandering naturally surface and erode public trust.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The number of voters in each constituency is often used as the justification for boundary changes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The average number of voters per Member of Parliament (MP) is not codified into law.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2020, the EBRC worked with a ratio of one MP to about 29,000 voters.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is very wide and creates the possibility that a constituency could be almost twice as large as another and still return the same number of MPs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, an SMC could have 20,000 to 38,000 voters while a five-member GRC could have 100,000 to 190,000 voters.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is unequal representation and unfair to voters.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2020, Sengkang GRC had 120,100 voters and elected four MPs, while East Coast GRC had 121,644 voters, only slightly more, but elected five MPs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yuhua SMC had 21,351 voters, while Bukit Panjang SMC had 35,437 voters.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means that the votes of Sengkang and Bukit Panjang voters counted for less compared to East Coast and Yuhua voters.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 1963, the EBRC adopted a rule allowing the numbers of voters in each electoral division to differ by no more than 20%.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The permitted deviation was increased to 30% in 1980.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This deviation should be narrower so that each electoral divisions has approximately equal numbers of voters.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is important as the electors' votes need to carry the same weight.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The electors' votes should be respected and not be unduly diluted by having larger deviation in each electoral division.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the United Kingdom (UK), for example, under the Parliamentary Constituencies Act 1986, there must be 650 MPs and the average number of voters per MP can only deviate by plus or minus 5%.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In Australia, the average number of voters per MP can only deviate by plus or minus 10% under the Commonwealth Electoral Act (No 2) 1973.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Putting aside the issue of unequal workload for each MP, we should adopt tighter limits on deviation to ensure that every Singaporean's vote carries the same weightage and is represented fairly in this House.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the interest of transparency, accountability and fairness to voters, PSP proposes the following changes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, upon formation of EBRC, announce the formation immediately and publish the current number of voters in each constituency based on boundaries in the last GE.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Further, identify the constituencies that require boundary changes based on fixed criteria.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, constituencies with the number of voters falling outside the specified range can have its boundaries changed.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The current range of 20,000 to 38,000 per MP is too wide, with the maximum number being 90% higher than, or nearly twice, that of the minimum.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means that some MPs are taking the load of nearly twice that of other MPs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As such, the maximum is limited to 22% higher than the minimum.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a fairer distribution of duties amongst MPs and fairer to voters in terms of their voting weightage.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, the boundaries of constituencies with number of voters within specified range cannot be changed unless justified on the basis of necessity due to an adjacent constituency having voters falling outside that specified range.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The basis for such changes must be published.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two, respect voters by reducing the potential for gerrymandering.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Gerrymandering is an attempt to manipulate the outcome of elections.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is an act of disrespect for voters.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead of working harder to make things better, serving the people better and being more responsive to the needs of the voters, gerrymandering seeks the easy way out of changing the rules.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The genuine concerns of voters are not addressed and respect for voters is eroded.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not acceptable and we should reduce the potential for gerrymandering in our system.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To achieve this, PSP makes the following proposal.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Just like houses and buildings have structural walls that cannot be demolished in renovations and non-structural walls that can be demolished, we propose the introduction of major boundaries and minor boundaries.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Major boundaries are meant to remain unchanged for many elections.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Each region bound by major boundaries could contain one or two GRCs and a few SMCs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These major boundaries should correspond closely to local ties and geographical considerations and could take reference from existing HDB town boundaries, URA planning area boundaries and postal district boundaries.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We propose that these major boundaries cannot be changed unless agreed to by a bipartisan committee.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The introduction of major boundaries that will not change frequently also make it easier for MPs to build community identities and bond.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Minor boundaries lie within the major boundaries and can be changed by EBRC based on the criteria mentioned earlier.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Suppose that a region enclosed by major boundaries is as follows: the number of voters was 200,000 in the previous GE and there was a five-member GRC with 140,000 voters plus two SMCs with 30,000 voters each.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Suppose that before the next GE, the number of voters changed as follows: (a) the number of voters grew to 220,000; (b) the number of voters in the GRC grew to 166,000 and the two SMCs dropped to 27,000 voters each.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under the proposed system, the boundaries of the two SMCs need not be changed as they are still within the range.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the boundaries for the GRC must change as it has gone beyond 33,000 per MP.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The GRC must now be served by six MPs instead of five.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By altering the minor boundaries, EBRC can change the GRC to either a five-member GRC + one SMC; or a four-member GRC + two SMCs; or a three-member GRC + three SMCs; or two three-member GRCs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The justification for the option chosen should be provided by EBRC.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will ensure a more level playing field by giving all political parties more time to prepare for the GE.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In response to a Parliamentary Question (PQ) earlier, Minister Chan Chun Sing had assured Parliament that "there will be sufficient time between the release of EBRC's report to the time of election." Does the Minister agree that a minimum of three months is a very reasonable time frame?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Four, enhancing independence in the composition, appointment and reporting structure of EBRC.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This starts with who gets to be appointed to EBRC.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is no law stating who gets to be appointed to EBRC, even though in recent years, EBRC has always consisted of the Cabinet Secretary, the chief executive officers (CEOs) of the Elections Department (ELD), HDB and the Singapore Land Authority (SLA), and the Chief Statistician.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are senior civil servants with deep domain knowledge that enable them to make decisions on how to redraw electoral boundaries in a practical way and we have no objection to them sitting on EBRC.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are concerns about potential conflict of interest for EBRC to report to the Prime Minister.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the interest of enhancing the independence of EBRC, PSP proposes that the membership of EBRC should be codified into law to prevent any future abuses.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the UK, for example, the Parliamentary Constituencies Act 1986 specifies that the Boundary Commissions are chaired by the Speaker of the House of Commons and the deputy chair must be a High Court Judge.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some legal constraints are necessary to prevent the appointment of partisan members onto the committee.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If EBRC is proposing changes to the major boundaries, then these changes must be approved by a committee to be chaired by the Speaker of Parliament by right of his office, but he will not play any part in the review.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The other members of the committee will be appointed by the President and comprise equal numbers of representatives from: one, the ruling party; and two, the other political parties that have won at least 5% of the votes at the previous GE.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For the sake of simplicity, I shall refer to this committee as "the bipartisan committee" within this debate.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the EBRC's proposed electoral boundary changes do not impact the major boundaries, then these changes do not need to be approved by a bipartisan committee.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the end of the process, the changes will be compiled into a report by EBRC and submitted to Parliament.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The report by the Boundary Commission for England contained a paragraph assuring that election results are not taken into consideration in the review of boundaries.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should do the same to enhance public trust.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The changes will be approved and implemented without modification by Parliament to ensure that the process remains fair and transparent.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Speaker, Sir, over the years, the Prime Minister has appointed the EBRC before a GE, and the establishment of the EBRC and the release of its report also signal the upcoming GE.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP is proposing this Motion today because we believe that there are many areas in our country's electoral boundaries review system that can be improved to enhance the transparency, independence, and fairness of the system.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since independence, the EBRC's reports have become increasingly concise and in recent years, the explanations for changes in constituency boundaries have been brief and vague.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This makes it difficult to determine whether the changes in electoral boundaries are solely due to changes in population and housing development.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, looking at the election results from 1988 to 2015, we find that the probability of opposition-held constituencies with a vote share between 40% and 50% disappearing in the next election is higher than constituencies where the opposition's vote share is below 40%.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Due to the overly concise nature of the EBRC's report, suspicions of unfair constituency delineation naturally arise.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the EBRC's report were more detailed, these doubts would naturally dissipate.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This results in significant disparities in voter representation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, in the 2020 general election, the number of voters in Sengkang GRC was almost the same as in East Coast GRC, but Sengkang GRC has four seats in Parliament while East Coast GRC has five seats.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The existing electoral boundaries mean that some MPs represent almost twice as many voters as other MPs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, PSP proposes that, in order to reduce the possibility of drawing the electoral boundaries unfairly, we should establish two types of electoral boundaries: major boundaries and minor boundaries.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Major boundaries can encompass multiple constituencies, and these boundaries should be stable and rarely changed to ensure community cohesion and reduce unfair constituency delineation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If changes to major boundaries are necessary, they should require the consent of a committee with equal representation from the ruling party and the opposition.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Minor boundaries are the boundaries between constituencies covered by major boundaries.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Minor boundaries can be adjusted based on changes in the population of constituencies.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fifthly, currently, there are no explicit regulations on the members of the EBRC.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To ensure fairness and transparency, we believe that legislation should stipulate that the EBRC should be chaired by a High Court Judge, with members being the CEO of ELD, HDB and SLA, as well as the Chief Statistician.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With that, I urge all hon Members to support the Motion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yes, Mr Speaker, I wish to participate in the debate, please.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Few Singaporeans have not privately wondered where the sea is when they look out of the window in Upper Serangoon or how the residents of Kaki Bukit have found themselves in four different GRCs over four different elections or why Sengkang, my home constituency, had its westernmost neighbourhood somewhat unceremoniously carved out from what had hitherto been a well-accepted division between the four "vales" of "River", "Compass", "Anchor" and "Fern".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Others have already explained why the present system comes across as inherently opaque and potentially unfair.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: First, I will explain how looking at the shape of boundaries alone does not tell us all that much.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Next, I will share that it is nevertheless possible to move away from the present status quo towards a more robust and, just as important, scientifically sound system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: With such a dizzying array of possibilities, it is plausible that potentially nonsensical shapes could emerge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This raises the perverse possibility that even oddly shaped maps could somehow turn out to be fair.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: After all, the outcome depends on the allocation of voters across space.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Nor can we rely solely on the magnitude of the win margins either.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: After all, disproportionate wins can result from very mild differences in geographic patterns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Just as crucially, first-past-the-post systems, such as ours, could potentially give rise to these outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The most recent Labour Party win in the UK is a fine example of this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But, that said, such arguments ultimately ring hollow because there are, indeed, ways to diagnose and treat the problem of gerrymandering.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Advances in mathematics, political science and economics offer the possibility of drawing credible electoral maps that will undoubtedly be better than the current opaque practices pursued by EBRC.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: One approach is to apply techniques in geometry to obtain compact districts that align well the sort of electoral geographies that make sense, not just mathematically, but also from intuitive notions of what should constitute a simply drawn, cohesive community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Such insights can be practically applied to actual data and, with the aid of computers, to new representative districts that can be derived in a completely reasonable timeframe.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: A second metric is to minimise what some political scientists have taken to calling an efficiency gap.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This approach simply asks that so-called wasted votes, the votes that would not be necessary for a winner to be declared in a given district, be kept as small as possible, taking into account voting shares across all districts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: A third relies more on game theoretic ideas to ensure fair division.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: One particularly promising strategy is to allow parties to take turns in either proposing divisions or rejecting unfavourable ones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This practice is actually less foreign than it seems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Elections in the 1950s in Singapore included representatives from several political parties and, in 1963, PAP itself invited opposition parties to submit proposals on delineating constituencies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Possibly the most promising set of tools rely on simulations based on repeated samples.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Such algorithms can generate sample districting plans under various constraints in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We might imagine a need to meet specific population targets and geographical compactness along with, of course, Ethnic Integration Policy considerations that are actually nevertheless more competitive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Just as important, these maps can be evaluated in advance, not merely after the fact, which means that they can be used by EBRC to draw out mathematically fair constituencies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: They can and have been profitably applied in real world situations, both as diagnostic tools as well as for the purposes of electoral reform.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Legal arguments relying on these techniques have gone all the way to various constitutional courts, where, for example, in Florida, proposals for eight of 27 proposed districts were struck down in 2023 on the basis of evidence presented.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In the state of Pennsylvania, an analogous Supreme Court ruling in 2018 declared violations of that state's constitution resulting from partisan congressional maps.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Perhaps most fundamentally, the principle behind these efforts is straightforward and consistent with the practice of many jurisdictions worldwide – to achieve impartiality by delegating the redistricting task to a truly independent electoral commission.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This has been adopted by, among other countries, Australia, Canada, India, Jordan, South Africa, South Korea, Thailand and the UK.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Computer packages to apply these solutions in a scalable way have been made available by researchers, including separate efforts by teams at Harvard and Tufts universities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: These can be adapted and adopted by our own EBRC to improve its own processes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The proposals I have offered get us much closer to a system that is both fair and, perhaps more importantly, perceived to be fair by the wider electorate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This, surely, is the sort of goal that everyone in this House and beyond would agree with.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Of course, perhaps we should take a step back and question the underlying political values that may have led us to even have to worry about the cancer of intentional gerrymandering.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If gerrymandering does truly become endemic, do we as a nation accept this?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Gerrymandering effectively means that the votes of those who happen to live in certain geographies are inadvertently given lesser weight simply by dint of the districting system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Do we wish to be known as a modern democracy that does not aspire to ensure that the voices of all our citizens be heard equally?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Any other Member wishes to join the debate?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, for decades, PAP has gained political advantage from the way that electoral boundaries have been drawn and redrawn.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, in a fair democratic political system, no party should gain such an advantage.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, Singapore should implement a politically impartial electoral boundary system based on international best practices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Third, if the 4G PAP were to implement such an impartial system, this would be in keeping with the promise flowing from the Forward Singapore exercise, that Singapore will operate under a refreshed social compact.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My first point is that PAP has gained political advantage from the drawing of electoral boundaries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Ms Hazel Poa has cited similar evidence in her speech on this Motion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the next GE in 1997, Braddell Heights was incorporated into Marine Parade GRC.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In GE2015, Joo Chiat was merged into Marine Parade GRC.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2015, the three SMCs where PAP had their smallest percentage of wins were incorporated into GRCs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As a matter of interest, these were all SMCs contested by WP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is really no need for me to say more about this or to give more examples because any reasonable person can tell that the examples cited are not coincidences.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is obvious that changes in the electoral boundaries of SMCs and GRCs have benefited PAP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My second point is that in a fair and democratic political system, no parties should benefit politically from the rejoining of boundaries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, Singapore should implement a politically impartial electoral boundaries system based on international best practices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would prevent a situation where any party, whether PAP now or some other party in future, benefits politically from the drawing of electoral boundaries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, and I quote, "If we want to avoid gerrymandering, any alteration of boundary lines to suit whoever is the Minister and his party, then let us have a Boundaries Commission".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, and I quote, "I am stating, as a proposition, that in any part of the world, and more especially in this part of the world, people who assumed the duties of Government are somewhat tempted to use the powers with which they are temporarily vested to weigh things permanently in their favour.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If we want to avoid gerrymandering, the drawing of boundary lines to include kampongs where one's supporters are and to exclude kampongs where one's opponents' supporters are, then let us have a proper Boundaries Commission.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Let the mechanics of it be by the Minister notifying it in the Gazette.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But let us have proper machinery to ensure that the working of Parliamentary democracy, this wholesale importation of western ideas of political organisation, is not perverted by feudalistic eastern ideas of personal survival".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Third, and I quote, "On principle, it is advisable to have the work of this Committee placed before all political parties.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If there had been no gerrymandering, it would be quite obvious to everybody and everybody would then be quite happy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But whether or not there has been an unconscious bias in the work of any official, so as to justify the allegations made by the Member for Serangoon, one can only judge from the vehemence of his allegations and the corresponding vehemence of the denials of the Chief Minister and the Chief Secretary.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Mr Lee talked about the possibility of unconscious bias, if a political party in power benefits from the redrawing of boundaries, whether that benefit has come about due to the unconscious or conscious bias of officials.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This can be taken care of through the two bodies proposed by Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In his speech in 1956, Mr Lee suggested that a Boundaries Commission be set up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And in his speech in 1957, he suggested that the work of such a Committee be placed before an all-party Committee.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Those measures proposed by Mr Lee are in line with those currently practiced by Australia, Canada and the UK, countries which practise the western ideas of political organisation that Mr Lee himself mentioned.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In these commonwealth countries, boundary revisions are decided by boundary commissions or committees which are independent of Government ministers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The commission of Canada and the UK include a high court judge appointed by the chief justice.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is variation in each country's process, but generally, the boundary commissions will publish proposed changes in the number of representatives and electoral boundaries based on set guidelines, which are formalised through legislation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The public and political parties are given the opportunity to provide feedback on these proposals before the boundary commissions make their final decisions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Ministers and Parliament cannot reject the decisions of the boundary commissions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the UK, the boundaries commissions for England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland consult the public before coming up with their final recommendations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In all these countries, there is a clear commitment to preventing political interference in the process of redrawing boundaries and to ensure the independence of the boundaries commission.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and the 4G PAP team were to implement such an impartial system, this would be in keeping with the spirit flowing from the Forward Singapore exercise that envisions Singapore operating under a refreshed social compact.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A commitment from the 4G leadership to an independent and de-politicised EBRC would be concrete manifestation through action.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the end, the choice is the PAP's.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They can continue with things as they are, or they can amend the law to entrench fairness into the electoral boundary system to protect future generations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even if they decide to retain the current system and not amend Singapore law, it is the PAP's choice whether to continue to accrue political advantage from the redrawing of electoral boundaries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This coming election is a chance for a new start, a refreshing of the social compact as the new Prime Minister has promised.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and the 4G leaders have the chance to change "politics as usual" in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I ask Prime Minister Lawrence Wong to take Singapore forward into a truly democratic political system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would enhance Singapore's world standing even further.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The international community and even fellow Singaporeans respects Singapore and our leaders for economic achievements and lack of corruption.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But there are asterisks when they assess our political system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As for the population of Singapore, changes that promote democratic participation will give the public greater confidence and pride in our political system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We in the Opposition, and I dare say ordinary Singaporeans, are asking Prime Minister Lawrence Wong to do the right thing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As Forward Singapore notes, Singapore is at a prime moment for change, and a functioning and robust social compact creates trust.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Keep your promise to Singaporeans to create a new and refreshed social compact.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Follow through with the Government's Forward Singapore exercise.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Bring Singapore forward with a fair electoral boundaries system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That is nothing more than aligning Singapore with international best practices.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: First, let me say that I would like to thank all the Members who have spoken on this and given your various suggestions and comments.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For Ms Hazel Poa, who has submitted her speech prior to ELD, we have also examined her suggestions very carefully.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The recent move to improve voter access for overseas Singaporeans is one such example.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: However, we cannot agree with the premise of this Motion.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: First, the Motion suggests that the current electoral boundary review process is not transparent and not fair.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Second, the Motion seeks to review the electoral boundary review process in the interests of political parties.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This process is meant to serve the interests of Singaporeans and not the interests of political parties.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The review is conducted by the EBRC, tapping on the specific expertise of its members, who include qualified senior civil servants with domain knowledge in the technical areas required for boundary delineation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Since 1958, the Prime Minister's terms of reference to the EBRC and its predecessors have been published.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The recommended delineation is presented to Parliament as a White Paper and this has been so since 1967.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The delineation of boundaries of electoral divisions comes down to a balance between the population and the geographical size of each electoral division.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Over time, with the movement of people and the development of new estates and towns, population densities in different areas will change.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The EBRC reviews the boundaries holistically, by taking into account such population shifts and housing developments while making sure that the boundaries make practical sense.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: A constituency must be an area that its MP or MPs can effectively represent and serve.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: At the same time, we strive to have some continuity and minimise the changes that could disrupt existing communities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: It is centred on the interests of voters and not the interests of political parties or candidates.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Government also gives reasonable notice of boundary changes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The past few GEs were called some one to three months after the release of EBRC's report.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: And as we have said before, we will seek to have sufficient time between the release of EBRC's report and the dissolution of Parliament, so that all political parties and candidates can make the necessary preparations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: ELD has been responding to Parliamentary and media queries on whether the Prime Minister has convened the EBRC for the coming GE.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: It will continue with this practice and will inform the public when the EBRC is convened.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: I will now address some other points raised by Ms Hazel Poa, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Ms Hazel Poa and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim have spoken about "suspicions of gerrymandering" and "reducing the potential for gerrymandering" and used the word "gerrymandering" quite a few times.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: First, let me touch on the EBRC's process and composition, which has allowed the committee to do its job independently and objectively.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The EBRC does not consult the PAP or any other political party.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Party politics do not come into this exercise.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The EBRC comprises senior civil servants with no party allegiances.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Therefore, unlike other countries where political parties are involved in the boundary drawing process, EBRC’s composition and processes are insulated from party politics.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Hence, we do not have the horse-trading and gerrymandering that have taken place in other countries.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: And I must say, if we get all political parties involved, present or future, it will politicise the whole process and not bring us forward, but bring us backwards.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Other jurisdictions that have done so continue to face allegations and doubts concerning the independence of their electoral boundary delineation process.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Their debate, instead, sinks into questions on who appoints the judge and whether the judge has any political leanings or bias.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The judiciary ends up getting drawn into the political debate and the judiciary is politicised.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Besides, there are no legal issues in the EBRC's work which require a judicial officer to weigh in.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: What is required is political neutrality, integrity and objectivity, which I trust all my Public Service officers have, whether they are in the EBRC or not, for them to discharge their duties without fear and favour.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The term "gerrymander" is almost as old as electoral politics.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: It originated in the US more than 200 years ago, in 1812.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Such allegations still persist, including in mature democracies, but the circumstances in Singapore are very different and should cause us to pause and ask ourselves, if indeed such "suspicions" and the "potential" of gerrymandering, as said, really exist and are possible.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: In other countries, gerrymandering happens when political parties manipulate boundaries to favour their supporters in specific areas.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This could be voters in urban or rural areas, or in specific ethnic enclaves.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The political parties assume that these voters, whom they consider their base, largely remain in the same areas, and therefore can have greater influence in the election outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: But in Singapore, every electoral division is more or less a microcosm of our nation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This is a result of our urban planning, where we do not want to have racial or religious enclaves in Singapore, nor do we have a rural-urban divide.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The voters in a given area are not always the same in every election, because they move around the whole island.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For those Members who have studied our electoral data, you would know.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Then there are many new first-time voters every electoral cycle.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Taken together, these two factors alone will add to a not insignificant churn of the respective constituencies' electoral roll, which calls into question any suggestion of the efficacy of attempts at gerrymandering.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: I should also point out that changes to the electoral boundaries have a greater impact on the incumbent parties and their MPs, given the substantial investment of time and effort by the MPs and their volunteers to engage and serve the residents, only to see them subsequently reassigned to another electoral division due to electoral boundary changes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Members may want to speak to Mr Sitoh Yih Pin on this after the debate.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Taking a step back, what we have heard from Ms Poa and others, and what they are really saying when she raises the point about gerrymandering comes down to this: we almost won this constituency, we think we can take it the next time, so do not touch it because we want to try again.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Paradoxically, if indeed the EBRC really takes these political considerations into account, then this would certainly qualify as gerrymandering.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Those principles and considerations are not different from what has been articulated in this House in the past.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: We know and all of us want more explanations from the EBRC.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: But we also have to strike a practical balance, so that our public officers are given the space to do their work independently and objectively, without fear or favour.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: That they should be allowed to provide recommendations without the fear that every change to the electoral boundaries will be politicised, if viewed unfavourably by certain political parties or individuals, no matter how minor those recommendations may be.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: And frankly, I do not think any amount of explanation is going to satisfy any political party, be they incumbent or opposition, and they may be unhappy with the boundary changes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: They are unhappy not because of the process but because of the outcome – they think they have lost out, that the map disadvantages them politically.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: And there is nothing that the EBRC can say about its process that will satisfy any political party because, as I have said, the EBRC does not take political interests into account.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Indeed, when the EBRC reviews the boundaries, it does so holistically – not only to take into account population shifts as mentioned, but also to balance the need for some continuity in community formation, as well as the objective of allowing the elected MP to serve the constituencies effectively.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This is an established process, which has worked and served us well.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Setting some fixed formula for the review or involving other persons who do not have the relevant expertise and knowledge to do the work, as suggested by Ms Hazel Poa, may instead undermine the effectiveness of the EBRC in carrying out its work.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: And the most important point is that, the involvement of political parties will also certainly politicise the process.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: And I think it will bring us backwards.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Ms Poa spoke about the need for the electors' votes to carry the same weight; she also suggested narrowing the range of voters per MP, and she cited the UK and Australia as examples.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: However, we must try to learn the right lessons in context.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: We must also present the comparison and lessons from other countries holistically and responsibly.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For context, while the UK and Australia examples may suggest a smaller margin of deviation per constituency, what Ms Poa should also highlight is that their number of electors per MP is two to three times that of ours.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Applying the same margin of deviation to a smaller base will certainly lead to more frequent and more drastic change to boundaries, because of our high rate of movement and change of addresses within a small city-state.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This may be the exact opposite of what Ms Poa may desire.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: A lower variation in the elector to MP ratio between constituencies is also not the only or overriding consideration.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: We can probably lower the percentage variation if we only have a few super constituencies with much larger populations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: But again, I do not think that is what Ms Poa is suggesting, nor do we think that it is a good outcome necessarily, because in absolute terms, voters would be served by fewer MPs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: An advantage of Singapore being a small country with a small population is that we can have much smaller constituencies, both in terms of population and area, which makes for a stronger connection between MPs and the area and voters that they serve.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Smaller constituency populations in absolute terms do mean that the percentage variation can be larger and we have to strive for a balance between the two that suits our context, rather than pursue one at the expense of the other.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: On the weight of each vote, we have also studied the systems in other countries very carefully.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: No electoral system in the world can definitively claim that every vote is exactly the same or near equal.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Even in established democracies today, we still have endless debates if the weight of every vote is the same.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For example, in the elections now ongoing, there are places which ask "why are smaller states having the same number of senators or representatives as bigger states?" Does that not mean that their votes are not of equal weightage?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: On Ms Poa's suggestion for major and minor boundaries, we have also studied it and we are not sure that it will resolve the fundamental issue when boundaries change.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Unlike big countries, with different states and provinces, we are a city-state with high mobility of our residents in every electoral cycle.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: To have "major boundaries" that cannot be changed and are immune to population shifts may not work out in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Then there will be the question of who and how should we delineate what constitutes major and minor boundaries?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: At the end of the day, what counts is the candidates that the party puts forth, and whether they are able to win the hearts and minds of Singaporeans to get elected into Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: At the GE2020, the formation of the new Sengkang GRC did not prevent the WP from winning that GRC, and that is why Assoc Prof Jamus Lim is here today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: It is not for me to tell parties and candidates how they should win the hearts and minds of our electorate.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: As Members have said, Singaporeans are wise people.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: They will know who has put in their hearts, day in day out, to serve them and I am sure they will cast their votes accordingly.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: To keep our electoral system working well, it must continue to be based on what is best for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Our system will continue to evolve, but we should not be changing the system, whether is it the electoral boundary review process or some other aspect, for the convenience or advantage of individual political parties.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: And when we study other people's system, we should also look at the system in entirety, rather than to pick and choose certain aspects that may or may not be able to be applied in context to ours, while neglecting other aspects in their systems as well.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: All political parties should not expect to keep or win seats because the boundaries are drawn one way or the other.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: And so, I urge all candidates to fight an election on substance.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Earn the trust of the electorate with concrete actions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Focus on how to serve the voters and gain their trust, wherever you choose to stand, rather than thinking about excuses for not being able to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Our electoral boundary review system is generally functioning well and seeks to ensure that voters distributed across Singapore are represented in Parliament in as fair a way as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: In other words, whether it has enabled the electorate to elect governments whom they trust and who serve them well.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: By those two tests, our system is reasonably good.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This is disastrous for our political system and for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Low trust countries are stuck in a vicious cycle, where the Government cannot do things that are urgent and necessary because the population does not trust them, and therefore they fail and the population’s trust in their leaders and system is further diminished, and we are on a downwards spiral.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: But we assure everyone that we will continue to evolve our electoral processes to better serve Singapore and Singaporeans first and foremost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When I sat there, listening to the long speech made by the Minister, I cannot help feeling that while we are here to say that there are some reasons to believe that the system is being politicised by the PAP, he in turn says that we are trying to politicise the whole system.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I think he has not answered the questions that we have raised or the doubts that we have raised.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why our electoral system or electoral boundary drawing has given rise to a number of phenomena or a number of things that we think is not normal?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We will only be convinced unless the Minister can explain why these things had happened.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, to reiterate what my colleague Hazel Poa, the Leader of the Opposition and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim have probably also raised; but I hope to raise a few questions and if the Minister can answer convincingly why this is so, then he will have a stronger case to say that we are politicising this whole debate.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can he explain why if there is no gerrymandering, then why are our constituency borders, the shape of our constituencies, some of them are very odd-shaped?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even the Minister agrees that it is better to have a more compact shape because the residents in the same areas should have a better environment to mix with one another.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And, of course, from an economics perspective, to maintain a constituency that is more compact, it is far more economical.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, why are some of our constituencies so odd-shaped?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Like the constituency that I am living in, Braddell Heights, Mr Speaker's constituency.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why is Braddell Heights under Marine Parade GRC, miles away?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My second question: the Minister also mentioned that the shape of a constituency or the current area of a constituency may be due to the urban planning that we have been doing.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yes, if that is the case, like what my colleague and other speakers have pointed out just now, why then is one HDB town divided, sub-divided amongst so many constituencies?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We would expect that if the urban planning is being done properly, then one HDB town will more or less be inside one constituency.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is the second question I wanted to ask the Minister.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And third, if there is no gerrymandering, then why have so many Singaporeans, although they have lived in the same place all their lives, experienced more than two times changing of constituencies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And fourth, what explains the disappearing of the SMCs, whereby the oppositions have done fairly well in an election?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And lastly, if there is no gerrymandering and no other political intention, then whenever there is a huge increase in population in one place, leading to a decline in the weightage of one vote, that means the discrepancy of the vote, we can actually address it quite speedily.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why is there a need to do that?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the Minister can answer them convincingly, then I think we can carry on with this debate and in more good faith.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I thought we should be seeking clarifications from you.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, I am not the EBRC.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, we are here to talk about the process and whether the process is right.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are not here to debate the decisions or recommendations of EBRC.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If you are trying to get me to explain on behalf of the EBRC, then I think you are trying to get me to say that I have some influence, direction or control over the EBRC.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Unfortunately, to disappoint you, I am not the EBRC.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, the Motion is about the process and whether the process should stay apolitical, to be run by the Public Service officers or do we want to go back in time and, like in other countries, where our process goes into a horse-trading between different political parties.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And even if we do that, what about new political parties that are formed?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Everyone will have a view on what they should and should not do, how the EBRC should or should not move or change the boundary.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, we are not here to explain what the EBRC does.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are here to talk about the review process.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: You can work it out mathematically and I am sure Ms Hazel Poa will agree.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Number three, you mentioned and you cited some examples of some people having to shift constituency although they stay in the same house.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That will always happen regardless of which system because when boundaries change, there will be some shifts.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And by your recommendations and your system, it will be much more and many more.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Minister Chan assured this House that there is in fact no intentional gerrymandering as pursued by the EBRC.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, my question is, what objections does the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) have to instructing the EBRC to adopt this approach in Singapore, given how it has been applied not just in theory but in practice by jurisdictions elsewhere?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First point, I am not sure I am an expert to distinguish what you refer to as "intentional" versus "unintentional".

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As I have mentioned in my speech, no system can ever claim that it is perfect nor will satisfy everyone who may choose to contest in an election.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The question is: what is the purpose of the EBRC and whom must it serve?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The fundamental question before us today is this: should the EBRC serve the interests of political parties or should the EBRC serve the interests of our people?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Should the EBRC, as its primary goal, serve the political interests of different parties or should the primary goal of the EBRC be to serve the interests of Singapore and Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And what are the goals of Singapore and Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, have an MP that can take care of them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, have an MP that can represent them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Third, have a Parliament that can form a functioning government that can take Singapore forward and look after Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are open to all kinds of tools, as suggested by Assoc Prof Jamus Lim.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Some of the ideas that the Member has mentioned and I listened carefully, but one of the Member's suggestions is quite interesting.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think, fundamentally, the Member would agree with us but he may also not like the result and it is this: that every electoral division should be a microcosm of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Member said that we should actually use mathematical models to adjust the population so that they reflect the national pattern.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First of all, if we use people's voting preference to adjust the model, would the Member not agree with us that that is precisely gerrymandering?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, if we indeed do that and every division is exactly the same, then every division should give the vote share to the incumbent that is roughly the same.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Is that the outcome that we are striving for?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, I think, have a care on how and what we learn from others and how we use models.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are open to exploring all kinds of models.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But at the end of the day, is fairness defined by the process or is fairness determined by the outcome as to whether it is favourable to me or not?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is the question that we have to think about.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: What I did say, in fact, was a suggestion about adjusting by mathematical methods the bounds, which is the shape of these electoral boundaries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is, in fact, uninformed by actual voting preferences which, as Minister Chan said, the EBRC has no access to.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister, do you need to respond to that?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Before that, just a point for the record.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I disagree with the Minister that the Motion, as filed by PSP, sows distrust.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If we do not discuss this issue in Parliament in a civil way, where do we do it?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I note that the Minister made a point about the presence of the term "political party" in the Motion and took issue with it at a few junctures in the course of his interventions and in the course of his speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: When asked by Mr JB Jeyaretnam whether there were plans to increase the number of electoral constituencies to Parliament and, if such, whether a committee had been set up and so on and so forth, the usual questions that we get, in view of the current system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Their report will be presented to this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: On previous occasions in 1967, 1971, 1976 and 1980, no political party served on the Committee.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Until there is a credible opposition party, this will continue to be the practice." Sir, I raise this to understand from the Minister whether the Minister's comments today are a significant point of departure in terms of the prospect of political parties ever serving on such an EBRC.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If it is, then we can have it on the record.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: A second clarification which I think we ought to have on the record is the question of gerrymandering.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Minister, in his speech, was very careful to phrase it in a particular way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: He said if – and correct me if I am wrong and if I am misquoting the Minister – the Minister said that if the EBRC takes notice or takes note of the close electoral contest in the previous elections in its work and it takes it into account, that would be gerrymandering.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Can I ask the Minister a simple question?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If you ask me, personally, I trust my civil servants to do their job objectively, professionally.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If you ask me, personally, I think they have served us well.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I cannot say what future governments may do.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I do not even know who may form the future governments.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And if a future government with a future Prime Minister thinks otherwise, then he explains to the House why they do so.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We can quote selectively from our previous Prime Ministers, previous MPs, but we have always prided ourselves as a system that we are very practical people.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We look at the issue at hand, see the needs of the country at its point in time and ask ourselves how do we evolve our system to keep pace with the needs of the time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have never let the past shackle us in thinking of new ideas, coming up with new processes that fit the needs of our time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I think that must be the spirit for us to keep progressing.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Even in established democracies today, they have so-called rules that they so-called stick to across time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They soon find themselves in trouble because those rules are not adequate to meet the needs of the time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I do not need to name any country.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There are many examples across the world for us to take a look at now.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the second point, I think I have explained the meaning of gerrymandering, what it means in other countries and whether it applies or not applies in our context.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I will leave it to Members of the House and the public to decide.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But okay, I just take it as that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But he is pointing out that today's debate is about the process.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I think it is not just about the process.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is about whether the current system is the most desirable system for the development of a fairer electoral system in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, I cannot imagine a situation where us, especially the Prime Minister who appoints the EBRC and also including all of us, we would accept a process that leads to an outcome that we find that is not desirable and that desirability is not measured by political considerations like, for example, whether it is good for the opposition or good for the ruling party.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But we can use certain parameters, like what Assoc Prof Jamus Lim has said.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We can use certain parameters like, for example, we should stipulate to EBRC that, preferably, we want the constituency to be a compact —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, you should not make another speech.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You can ask your clarifications directly to Minister Chan.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, we can give a parameter to the EBRC that we want the constituency to be more compact.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Given that, does the Minister agree that it is not just about the process that we are arguing today?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is about the outcome and this outcome does not necessarily be a political outcome that we are aiming for.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We are talking about a more rational boundary drawing in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I am glad that Mr Leong says that we are here to talk about the process and not the outcome.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Maybe Mr Leong can clarify what does outcome mean.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Is outcome the boundaries or is outcome whether a certain party, a certain candidate, wins or loses?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Is the EBRC responsible for WP winning Sengkang GRC in the last GE?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Do we pin that outcome on the EBRC?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The EBRC's outcome is a set of boundaries, Sengkang Town.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ultimately, Sengkang voters choose who they want to represent them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But, Sir, if I may just move one step back, as I have to reiterate this point.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The mark of success of how we evaluate a political system is whether it is fit for purpose, it commands the trust and respect of its people so that the country can progress together.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Very often, perhaps in this Chamber, we are all very seized with who wins, who loses.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At the end of the day, it must be Singapore and Singaporeans who win.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It must be that we have a functioning Parliament that can produce good governance in service of our people and nation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And it is on that note and that is the real outcome that we are looking for.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The outcome is not whether your party wins or my party wins.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can I ask the Minister did we propose anything that is targeted at aiming for a particular political outcome?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We did not propose any of that and we do not know what will be the political outcome because it all depends on the electorate.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But we have proposed concrete ideas as to why we think the electoral boundaries should be drawn with more objective parameters and I pointed out one just now to you, whether we can give the parameter to the EBRC that we want more compact constituencies?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, I want the Minister to confirm whether we actually aim for a political outcome in our debate today or did we actually put up ideas to say that we are asking for a more objective way of drawing the boundaries?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, maybe you should also respond to the Minister's questions to you, so that we can progress and come to a finality on the debate.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Did he say a process or an outcome?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I think he mentioned about your definition of an outcome.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We do not know what the political results will be, but definitely, we would like to see, for example, our constituencies being more compact, where the residents of one constituency are living closer to one another.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Like now, I live in Braddell Heights, I do not know my fellow constituents in the far end of the other part of Marine Parade, for example.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I am sure we can provide more parameters, but just answer me.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: This parameter is what I mean by the outcome that we are aiming for.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I am thoroughly confused now, as to whether the Member is suggesting that the Prime Minister give more specific instructions to the EBRC or the Member would like the Prime Minister to allow the EBRC to do its work objectively, with some basic instructions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Because it sounds like, now, we have to have the Prime Minister tell the EBRC the definition of compactness.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It sounds like we want the Prime Minister to give the EBRC even more specific instructions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I am sure, if the Prime Minister does that, the Prime Minister will be accused of interfering unnecessarily in the process of the EBRC.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, I think the Prime Minister will do what he needs to do to give the broad outlines and guidelines to the EBRC.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will leave the EBRC to do their work, professionally and objectively.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Sometimes, the more we interfere, the more we fall into this trap to make it a politically-motivated process.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
